content.aim: To construct and verify the operation of a Half Adder circuit built from basic logic gates.
objectives: To understand how a Half Adder produces SUM and CARRY outputs from two single-bit inputs, A and B. To build the circuit shown in Figure 3 (Half Adder) on a breadboard using standard logic-gate ICs. To verify the circuit's operation by completing a truth table. To retain the constructed circuit for use in the Full Adder experiment (Experiment 4).
apparatus: Logic gate ICs (AND and XOR-equivalent gates)

theory.text: A Half Adder adds two single bits, A and B, producing two outputs: SUM and CARRY. The SUM output is the Exclusive-OR (XOR) of the inputs, while the CARRY output is their logical AND: SUM = A ⊕ B CARRY = A · B In Figure 3, this is realised using two AND gates and an inverting (“1”) stage arranged to produce the XOR function for SUM, together with a separate AND gate that produces CARRY directly from A and B.

procedure: Wire the logic gate ICs on the breadboard as shown in Figure 3, and power them with 5 V.
Apply all four combinations of A and B using switches.
Observe the SUM and CARRY outputs using a logic probe or LED indicators.
Record the results in the truth table and retain the circuit for Experiment 4.
precautions: Switch off the power supply before changing any wiring.
Ensure IC pins are correctly oriented (align the pin-1 notch) before insertion.
Do not leave unused gate inputs floating; tie them to a defined logic level.
Use current-limiting resistors for any LED indicators.
Verify the +5 V and ground rails before powering the board.
content.discussion: The measured truth table matched the theoretical Half Adder function exactly: SUM followed the XOR pattern and CARRY followed the AND pattern for all four input combinations. A key limitation of the Half Adder is that it has no carry-in input, so it can only add two bits at a time and cannot, on its own, be chained to add multi-bit numbers beyond the least-significant bit position.
content.conclusion: The constructed circuit correctly implements the Half Adder Boolean functions, SUM = A ⊕ B and CARRY = A · B, matching the theoretical truth table. This circuit forms the basic building block used in Experiment 4 to construct a Full Adder.
